source: Jakubuv & Urban (2017) ENIGMA: Efficient Learning-based Inference Guiding Machine
finding: First practical learned given-clause guidance inside E. A linear classifier (LIBLINEAR, hashed symbol features) labels clauses as in-proof or not, and its score is mixed into E's clause weight function.
numbers: CASC 2016 AIM, 200 test problems, 180 s: E strategy S0 alone 22; S0 plus classifier 41; all guided strategies together 52; Vampire 47 (3x180 s). Training: 1020 problems, 239 solved by S0, 337 after bootstrapping; 6821 positive vs 219012 negative clauses; 97.6% train accuracy; about 10 microseconds per clause.
quote: the theorem prover automatically takes into account thousands of previous successes and failures
limits: Single narrow domain (algebra AIM, consistent symbol names); trained and tested on the same problem family.
agent_relevance: Learned scoring of the next item to expand beats the hand heuristic when the scorer is cheap and the problem family is stable. Scorer cost must stay near the cost of a step.

source: Jakubuv & Urban (2017) ENIGMA: Efficient Learning-based Inference Guiding Machine (looping and boosting)
finding: Positive clauses repeated 10 times in training data to favour recall. Overall accuracy drops but positives are found far more often.
numbers: Overall accuracy 98% to 93%; accuracy on positive clauses 12.5% to 81.8%; solved 5 more competition problems (4 unsolved by Vampire), total 57 in 600 s; 16 problems in total that Vampire did not solve.
limits: Single benchmark; hand-tuned weights and frequencies (grid over 12 frequencies and 9 weight values).
agent_relevance: Rare-positive imbalance is the real problem for learned guidance. Reward finding the rare useful step, not average correctness.

source: Loos, Irving, Szegedy, Kaliszyk (2017) Deep Network Guided Proof Search
finding: First deep nets (CNN, WaveNet-style) to rank clauses inside E on Mizar. Pure net guidance was too slow; a hybrid and then a two-phase switch to E's Auto heuristic was needed.
numbers: Mizar, 57,882 FOL theorems, 32,521 (56%) already had ATP proofs; 82,718 training proofs of 29,325 conjectures. Best clause classifier accuracy 81.5% (WaveNet 640 with dropout) on a 50-50 split. On 25,361 hard theorems, guided runs proved 7.36% (1,866), lifting the ATP-proved share from 56% to 59%.
limits: Per-clause net evaluation dominates run time; without premise selection or the switch guided runs were worse.
agent_relevance: A learned judge inside a loop must be amortised. Evaluation cost per step can erase the gain from fewer steps.

source: Loos et al. (2017) Deep Network Guided Proof Search (Table 3 negative result)
finding: Unswitched hybrid network guidance proved FEWER hard theorems than unguided E, because the network is slow.
numbers: Hard theorems proved: without premise selection unguided 145 vs guided hybrid 137; with premise selection unguided 458 vs guided hybrid 383.
limits: Fixed wall-clock budget; later work with faster models reversed this.
agent_relevance: Honest control: a smarter step selector is not a win if each selection costs much more than a plain step. Count compute, not steps.

source: Chvalovsky, Jakubuv, Suda, Urban (2019) ENIGMA-NG
finding: Replaced the linear model with gradient-boosted trees and recursive neural networks inside E. Trees and nets complement each other and the linear model; the original hand strategy becomes redundant in the union.
numbers: MPTP2078 solved counts: baseline S 1086; guided variants range 1115 to 1256 (best is boosted trees combined with S). On 232 newly solved problems true-positive rate falls about 15% and true-negative rate about 20% on unseen test data vs training.
limits: Column labels in the extracted results table are ambiguous; MPTP2078 only (symbol-name dependent); same library for train and test.
agent_relevance: Ensembles of different learned scorers solve different problems. Agreement on training proofs overstates test quality, so held-out checks matter (G3).

source: Jakubuv & Urban (2019) Hammering Mizar by Learning Clause Guidance
finding: Scaled ENIGMA with XGBoost to the whole Mizar library, iterating prove, learn, prove. One learned single strategy beats the hand-evolved portfolio.
numbers: Mizar problems solved in 10 s: baseline S 14,933; best looped strategy 25,397 (+70.0%). At 60 s: 26,107 vs the six-strategy hand portfolio 22,068 (+18.3%). Vampire CASC portfolio at 300 s: 27,842. 1296 hard problems (unsolved before) solved. Training matrix 63M examples x 65,536 features.
limits: Same library for train and test; Vampire still ahead with longer time; features are hashed.
agent_relevance: A looped generate, verify, retrain cycle gave 70% on one library. It works because the prover is a perfect verifier of what was proved.

source: Crouse et al. (2019/2021) TRAIL: A Deep Reinforcement Learning Approach to First-Order Logic Theorem Proving
finding: Reinforcement learning from scratch (no seed proofs) guiding the Beagle saturation prover. Beats earlier RL provers but still loses to hand-tuned E.
numbers: Problems solved, M2k / MPTP2078: TRAIL 1561 / 910; plCop 1359 / 782; rlCop 1235 / 733; E solves the most. TRAIL +202 over best RL rival on M2k and +128 on MPTP2078; 22% relative gain over its base Beagle on MPTP2078; 11% loss training MPTP and testing M2k, 3% loss the reverse.
limits: Limit 2000 steps and 100 s; reports best iteration on the training set; GNN vectorisers not shown to repay their cost.
agent_relevance: Even a learned-from-scratch step chooser lags the engineered heuristic baseline. Treat learned guidance as an add-on, not a replacement.

source: Jakubuv, Chvalovsky, Olsak, Piotrowski, Suda, Urban (2020) ENIGMA Anonymous: Symbol-Independent Inference Guiding Machine
finding: Symbol-independent guidance: GBDT on arity-based features and a GNN that scores clauses in batches with the context of already selected clauses. GBDT beats GNN in later iterations even though the GNN has better test accuracy.
numbers: Mizar40: union of twelve ENIGMA strategies 28,247 problems; plus base S 28,271; plus eight new strategies 29,130, including 2,109 hard Mizar40 problems unsolved before, in 200 s. Feature collisions about 1% (symbol-independent) vs 0.42% (symbol-dependent).
quote: The GNN models report better testing accuracy, but their ATP performance is not as good.
limits: Mizar-derived MPTP data only.
agent_relevance: Classifier test accuracy did not predict prover performance. Judge by problems solved under a budget, never by accuracy alone.

source: Suda (2021) Improving ENIGMA-Style Clause Selection While Learning From History
finding: Recursive neural net on clause derivation history inside Vampire. Only the layered clause selection integration (second queue at a 1:2 ratio) improved on the baseline; relying heavily on advice hurt.
numbers: SMT-LIB subset, real time: baseline 734 problems; best guided 141% of baseline; layered 1:2 ratio gives 137% and gains 430 problems the baseline missed; abstract headline 41% improvement; solved count rose as less advice was taken.
quote: only the layered clause selection integration is able to improve on the performance of the baseline strategy
limits: One SMT-LIB subset.
agent_relevance: Mix learned and fixed selection rather than handing over fully. Matches G1: use the extra judge only where it helps and keep the plain queue.

source: Chvalovsky, Jakubuv, Olsak, Urban (2021) Learning Theorem Proving Components
finding: Contextual evaluation: learn which components (clusters) of the clause graph matter and score clauses within that context instead of in isolation.
numbers: Clustering the unsolved training problems: k-means k=2 gives 67 newly solved, k=3 gives 78, soft k-means k=2 gives 63 (of about 32k unsolved).
limits: Small absolute gains; Mizar-derived data.
agent_relevance: Splitting a problem into components and solving each in isolation is a cheap decomposition move for hard tasks.

source: Piepenbrock, Urban, Korovin, Olsak, Heskes, Janota (2022) Machine Learning Meets the Herbrand Universe
finding: A neural net proposes ground instances of first-order clauses and a SAT plus congruence solver checks them. Learned proposal, exact check.
numbers: 113,332 Mizar clausal problems; first randomized grounding run solves 3,897, rising to 7,790 over the first 100 runs; about 6.0 instances needed per solved problem; 3.9 of them (about two thirds) contain a skolem symbol.
limits: The randomized baseline is weak; the learned system tested on M2K only.
agent_relevance: Guess candidates with a model, verify exactly with a solver: the same shape as a propose-then-check loop.

source: Gleiss & Suda (2020s) Layered Clause Selection for Saturation-Based Theorem Proving
finding: Layered selection groups clauses by a numeric feature (theory reasoning, goal relatedness, Avatar split dependencies, Horn closeness) and boosts a basic heuristic. Implemented in Vampire; no learning.
numbers: TPTP: base 9,108 solved (rerun gives 9,204); layered single-feature strategies solve about 9,160 to 9,526 (+52 to +417 over base); the union of th+av+sl+pl reaches 10,297 (+1,189). On SMT-LIB union gains about 3,226 over base. Best split-ratio tuning gains +103 (TPTP, ratio 6:1) and +78 (SMT-LIB, ratio 1:1).
limits: Table text partly garbled in extraction; paper read from a local PDF, no stable URL recorded. Run-to-run variation 9,512 vs 9,525 on the same strategy (non-deterministic environment).
agent_relevance: Hand-built structural queues give diversity cheaply; the gain is largest in the union, again favouring many different selectors over one.

source: Chvalovsky, Suda, Urban (2026) Teaching Vampire New Tricks: An Experimental Study of Neural Clause Selection (boost)
finding: Neural clause selection in Vampire (default strategy) boosts every ITP-derived benchmark but the gain is smaller on unseen test problems.
numbers: Default to boosted problems solved: TPTP 8,511 to 10,864 of 15,500 (+27.6%); Mizar40 train 4,733 to 10,098 (+113.4%), test 1,543 to 3,101 (+101.0%); Isabelle test 2,178 to 2,715 (+24.7%); CoqHammer train 2,813 to 9,799 (+248.3%), test 399 to 772 (+93.5%).
limits: Strict train/test split shrinks the gain (CoqHammer); TPTP had no held-out split.
agent_relevance: Learned guidance gains are real but partly in-distribution. Report held-out gains only.

source: Chvalovsky, Suda, Urban (2026) Teaching Vampire New Tricks: An Experimental Study of Neural Clause Selection (no transfer)
finding: A model trained on one benchmark family does worse than the plain default on other families as it specialises. The authors suspect it learns encoding quirks more than how to control a prover.
numbers: A TPTP-trained model fell below the default on Mizar40 once the 1,840 Mizar-derived problems were removed. A single model trained on all four sets reached 100.0% (TPTP), 99.4% (Mizar40), 101.4% (Isabelle) and 95.3% (CoqHammer) of each dedicated model.
quote: a clear negative answer to the question about knowledge transfer
limits: Cross-set failure is explained by different clause encodings (type guards vs type tags), not proven by ablation.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: a learned selector is tied to its input format. A scaffold with learned parts must be re-checked per task family.

source: Chvalovsky, Suda, Urban (2026) Teaching Vampire New Tricks: An Experimental Study of Neural Clause Selection (strategies and portfolios)
finding: Boost does not stack fully with strategy portfolios: gains shrink when complementary strategies are present.
numbers: Five-strategy portfolio: strategy 1 boosted 9,265 to 11,264 (+21.6%); union of the five defaults 10,719 vs 12,207 boosted (+13.9%); one model trained on all five gives +23.8% average boost and 12,195 combined coverage; strategy 1 gains 15.7% from strategies 2-5 unboosted but only 8.4% once boosted; schedule coverage at 32,000 Mi 76.1% vs 67.8% (+12.2%), overall +4.1%.
limits: One hardware budget; Vampire only.
agent_relevance: Diminishing returns: a better single solver lowers the value of running several diverse ones. Relevant to best-of-N versus one good scaffold.

source: Tafjord, Dalvi Mishra, Clark (2021) ProofWriter: Generating Implications, Proofs, and Abductive Statements over Natural Language
finding: A T5 generator iterated one inference step at a time (a neural forward-chaining loop) makes proofs that reflect actual model steps and generalises to unseen depths better than all-at-once generation.
numbers: RuleTaker D5 proof accuracy: ProofWriter 96.2% overall vs PRover 87.1%; at depth 5, 86.4% vs 65.1%; answer accuracy about 99.3% for both. Birds-Electricity out of domain, proof correctness: iterative 97.0% vs all-at-once 84.5% vs PRover 80.5%; answer accuracy iterative 97.0% vs all-at-once 85.5% vs PRover 86.5%.
quote: iterating a 1-step implication generator results in proofs that are highly reliable
limits: Templated synthetic English, small domain; this is forward chaining, not resolution.
agent_relevance: One step at a time under a fixed outer loop kept accuracy at depth; supports program-controlled step loops.

source: Olausson, Gu, Lipkin, Zhang, Solar-Lezama, Tenenbaum, Levy (2023) LINC
finding: The LLM only translates text to first-order logic; Prover9 (a resolution prover) decides. Ten samples, majority vote over prover answers.
numbers: ProofWriter balanced subset with LINC: GPT-3.5 96.4%, GPT-4 98.3%; StarCoder+ (15.5B) with LINC beats GPT-3.5 CoT by 38 points and GPT-4 CoT by 10 points. FOLIO: StarCoder+ 56.0% vs 41.8% CoT; GPT-3.5 62.6% vs 54.9%; GPT-4 LINC 72.5% vs CoT 75.3% (McNemar p=0.58, not significant).
limits: Gain vanishes on FOLIO for the strongest model. FOL syntax errors in 38% (StarCoder+), 24% (GPT-3.5), 13% (GPT-4) of generations; missing implicit facts such as Person(Harry) is a main failure.
agent_relevance: A resolution prover as exact checker behind a translation step helps weak models a lot and strong models little. Errors move from reasoning to translation.

source: Olausson et al. (2023) LINC (scratchpad ablation and depth)
finding: Writing the FOL but letting the model predict the answer itself, with no prover call, did not help; the prover call is what matters. LINC accuracy holds across proof depth while baselines fall to chance.
numbers: StarCoder+ baselines flat near chance at all depths; GPT-3.5 baselines at chance beyond depth 1; GPT-3.5 with LINC near perfect at all depths; GPT-4 with LINC at or near ceiling through the maximum depth.
limits: ProofWriter is synthetic with short sentences, which suits formalisation.
agent_relevance: Do not let the model finish its own formal step; hand the finishing step to code (G5).

source: Pan, Albalak, Wang, Wang (2023) Logic-LM: Empowering LLMs with Symbolic Solvers for Faithful Logical Reasoning
finding: Translate to symbols, run a solver (Prover9 for FOL tasks, other solvers for other tasks), self-refine the translation from solver error messages.
numbers: Accuracy standard / CoT / Logic-LM, GPT-4: ProofWriter 52.67 / 68.11 / 79.66; FOLIO 69.11 / 70.58 / 78.92; PrOntoQA 77.40 / 98.79 / 83.20; LogicalDeduction 71.33 / 75.25 / 87.63; AR-LSAT 33.33 / 35.06 / 43.04. Average gain 39.2% over standard and 18.4% over CoT (GPT-3.5).
limits: On PrOntoQA GPT-4 CoT (98.79) beats Logic-LM (83.20). Executable rate before refinement: FOLIO 79.9% (GPT-4), AR-LSAT 32.6%.
agent_relevance: A solver wins on hard multi-step tasks and loses where CoT is already near ceiling. Use an external check where plain reasoning fails, not by default (G1).

source: Pan et al. (2023) Logic-LM (self-refinement and depth)
finding: Self-refinement from solver error text raises the share of runnable formalisations, but accuracy stalls after round 1.
numbers: Executable rate gain averages +5.01 points; FOLIO GPT-3.5 66.7% to 84.3%, GPT-4 79.9% to 85.8%; AR-LSAT GPT-4 32.6% to 39.8%. Logic-LM advantage over CoT grows with required hops (300 balanced ProofWriter examples per depth bucket).
limits: Feedback is syntax errors only, not semantic mismatch; accuracy stagnates in later rounds.
agent_relevance: Revise from real solver output (G2). Syntax feedback fixes form, not meaning.

source: Ye, Chen, Dillig, Durrett (2023) SATLM: Satisfiability-Aided Language Models Using Declarative Prompting
finding: The LLM writes a declarative specification and a SAT/SMT solver answers. Compared with program-aided LMs and chain of thought on 8 datasets.
numbers: code-davinci-002 greedy, columns GSM-Sys/GSM/Algebra/LSAT/BoardgameQA/CLUTRR/ProofWriter: SATLM 69.4/71.8/77.5/35.0/79.4/68.3/99.7; CoT 46.5/62.7/53.6/23.5/60.7/40.8/80.1; PAL 43.4/72.7/52.3/-/-/58.9/83.7. With self-consistency SATLM reaches 37.4% on LSAT (prior SoTA 30.9%); +23% over PAL on the hard GSM subset.
limits: Uses a SAT/SMT prover, not a resolution prover; parse errors are unrecoverable; on plain GSM SATLM only matches PAL.
agent_relevance: Declarative spec plus exact solver beats imperative code on constraint problems: the model states facts, the solver searches.

source: Feng, Xu, Hao, Sharma, Shen, Zhao, Chen (2023) Language Models can be Logical Solvers (LoGiPT)
finding: Fine-tune an LLM on a solver's reasoning traces so it imitates the solver without a parse step and removes parse failures.
numbers: ProofWriter / PrOntoQA accuracy: LoGiPT Vicuna-13B 81.17 / 96.40; CodeLlama-13B base 89.50 / 95.60; CodeLlama-13B instruct 81.67 / 96.20. For comparison Logic-LM GPT-4 79.66 / 83.20 and GPT-4 CoT 68.11 / 98.79.
limits: Trained on same dataset families; mixed training gave slightly lower test scores (about 79 to 81 on ProofWriter).
agent_relevance: A model can learn to mimic a symbolic loop, but without an external guarantee; contrast with calling the real prover.

source: Han et al. (2022, rev. 2024) FOLIO: Natural Language Reasoning with First-Order Logic
finding: Human-written benchmark with FOL annotations verified by an inference engine; a subset challenges GPT-4.
numbers: 1,430 examples (unique conclusions) over 487 premise sets; v3 revised Oct 2024.
limits: Abstract page only; model numbers not read here.
agent_relevance: Benchmark behind most LINC and Logic-LM numbers; the real-language case where translation errors dominate.

source: Qi et al. (2025) Large Language Models Meet Symbolic Provers for Logical Reasoning Evaluation (ProverGen, ProverQA)
finding: LLM plus symbolic prover generate a first-order logic benchmark with intermediate steps; frontier LLMs struggle on it even with chain of thought; fine-tuning Llama3.1-8B-Instruct on the generated training set helps in and out of distribution.
numbers: No accuracy figures read (abstract page only).
limits: Abstract only; prover not named on the page.
agent_relevance: Provers can make verified training and test data, not only answer questions.

source: Search note (2026-11-01): no LLM-as-clause-selector study found
finding: One web search for LLMs steering superposition or given-clause selection returned only the ENIGMA family and the 2026 Vampire study; no 2024-2026 paper that puts an LLM in the clause-selection loop was found. Budget exhausted before a second search.
numbers: none
limits: Absence of evidence from one search plus failed API rate limits (arXiv, Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex all returned 429 or empty), not proof of absence.
agent_relevance: Gap: LLM inside the saturation loop is untested in what we found; the only LLM uses are translation front ends (LINC, Logic-LM) and trace imitation (LoGiPT).
